# Promoting constructive feedback on preprints with the FAST principles

## Authors

- Sandra Franco Iborra<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-7385-657X](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7385-657X))
- Jessica Polka<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-6610-9293](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6610-9293))
- Iratxe Puebla<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0003-1258-0746](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1258-0746)) †

### Affiliations

1. ASAPbio San Francisco United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Ensuring that public feedback on preprints is focused, appropriate, specific and transparent (or FAST) will help to develop a thriving culture for reviewing and commenting on preprints.

## FAST: Focused, Appropriate, Specific and Transparent

If we want to promote public feedback on preprints, we need to articulate the behaviors that reflect the constructive and inclusive interactions we would like to see. With that goal, we convened a Working Group that included researchers, editors, preprint review platforms and funders to discuss two questions: what practices enable the benefits of public feedback on preprints? What are the cultural barriers that prevent us from embracing public preprint review, and how do we overcome these barriers? The output of the Working Group are the FAST principles, a set of 14 principles clustered around four broad themes (Franco Iborra et al., 2022; Figure 1):

![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/78424/elife-78424-fig1-v1.jpg)

**Figure 1.:** The 14 FAST principles are clustered around four broad themes: focused, appropriate, specific and transparent. See Franco Iborra et al., 2022 for more details.

The FAST principles include existing advice on how to engage with journal peer review, but they also go further to reflect the public nature of comments on preprints, the possibility to comment without an editor, and the involvement of a wider community. We envision the community as an important stakeholder with the ability to engage and interact with the comments provided by authors and reviewers. Of course, just like authors and reviewers, the community has a responsibility to ensure that all exchanges remain constructive, inclusive and positive.

Different organizations can make use of the FAST principles in different ways. The platforms that host commentary and reviews on preprints can incorporate the principles into their framework for contributors, and use them as part of any moderation processes they have in place for posted reviews.

While most journals already have their own resources for authors and reviewers, editors may find that the FAST principles contain useful elements (such as, for example, guidance for authors on how to respond to comments from reviewers). For journals seeking to bring feedback on preprints into their editorial process (O’Grady, 2021), the principles provide a framework for selecting preprint reviews that are suitable for the journal’s editorial process. In addition, for journals that post reviews alongside preprints, such as eLife and EMBO Journal (eLife, 2021; Pulverer and Lemberger, 2019), the principles can guide what elements of the review are most relevant to post publicly with the preprint.

Institutions seeking to recognize peer review activities, including the peer review of preprints, in staff performance reviews could signal that for reviews of preprints to be eligible for recognition, they must have been completed in line with the principles.

And most importantly, we hope that the FAST principles are also a valuable resource for researchers. Early-career researchers seeking to build review skills, including students participating in courses on peer review, could be encouraged to use the principles when writing their reviews (as in the course Biochemistry 200A at the University of California San Francisco), as could participants in preprint journal clubs.

Of course, we do not expect the culture of public commenting on preprints to change overnight. Most of those who have previously participated in peer review have only done so in the context of a closed process run by a journal, where their comments were only seen by the editor and authors, and where most often comments were not signed. Moving the conversation into the public space means being much more proactive about how we develop our review, what biases we may have, and what choices of language we make to prevent misinterpretation. It may mean putting in that bit of extra effort when drafting our comments, but given the overall benefits of public feedback on preprints, we view this as a worthwhile investment.

## Looking forward

New platforms and communities are developing around the review of preprints, and it is likely that new approaches and tools will allow us to react to and comment on preprints in ways that are not possible today. The norms around public commentary on preprints are still fluid, but it is important to set the foundations for a constructive and inclusive culture at this early stage. The FAST principles outline behaviors that will encourage and lead to such a culture. And as activities around preprint feedback grow in visibility, scope and variety, we expect that standards will also evolve, and we look forward to seeing the principles develop to meet the changing needs of the community.

Preprints have brought researchers new freedom for how and when they communicate their research. By enabling new ways of public interaction, preprints also allow researchers to make new choices about how they engage in feedback and scientific discourse. In the context of a preprint, feedback is focused on the science, and not on the requirements of a particular journal. This gives an individual the opportunity to comment on a specific aspect of a preprint, or work in a group to provide a collective review. Importantly, by encouraging this public interaction and articulating what we value in preprint feedback, we can also enable new ways to reward reviews as scholarly contributions in their own right.

Journal peer review is valued by the scientific community, but it is seldom a conversation. Scientists value interactions with their peers about their work, and they gather feedback and ideas from face-to-face conversations, email enquiries, discussions at conferences and, sometimes, social media. The spirit of the FAST principles is to open a new avenue for this communication through preprint feedback. An added benefit is that it will give both the broader scientific community and the general public a chance to participate. We invite all members of the scientific community to be part of this conversation.

results.result: A Working Group comprising researchers, editors, preprint review platforms, and funders was convened to develop the FAST principles. The output was a set of 14 principles organized around four themes (Focused, Appropriate, Specific, Transparent) that build upon existing journal peer review guidance while addressing the unique aspects of public preprint commentary.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C3 provide factual documentation of the Working Group convening and its output (supported by citation and Figure 1). Claims C4 and C5 describe the content and scope of the principles based on the authors' direct knowledge of their development. These claims collectively establish the creation and nature of the FAST principles.

results.result: The FAST principles have multiple potential applications across the scholarly ecosystem, including use by preprint platforms for moderation, journals for editorial processes, institutions for recognizing peer review activities, and educational settings for training early-career researchers. One concrete example is provided: use in the Biochemistry 200A course at UCSF.
results.evaluation: Most claims (C8-C10, C12-C14) are speculative about potential future applications using modal verbs like 'can' and 'could.' Only C15 provides a concrete example of actual implementation. While C11 is factually supported by citations, the broader claim about widespread adoption and effectiveness lacks empirical validation. The result describes possibilities rather than demonstrated outcomes.

results.result: The FAST principles are proposed to help develop a thriving, constructive, and inclusive culture for preprint review at a time when norms around public preprint commentary are still fluid and foundations need to be established.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C23 are speculative about the future impact of the FAST principles without empirical evidence of their effectiveness. While C21 accurately describes the current state (fluid norms) and C22 makes a normative argument for establishing foundations, no data is provided demonstrating that the FAST principles will actually achieve the stated cultural transformation. This is a hypothesis requiring future validation.

results.result: Traditional journal peer review has been conducted as a closed, anonymous process, and transitioning to public preprint feedback requires greater proactivity regarding review development, bias awareness, and language choices. Despite requiring extra effort, this transition is worthwhile given the overall benefits of public feedback.
results.evaluation: Claim C16 accurately describes traditional peer review practices based on established knowledge. Claim C17 makes a logical inference about the implications of moving to public review. Claim C18, while speculative about benefits, is presented as the authors' reasoned position. Together, these claims provide a coherent rationale for the cultural shift being proposed.

results.result: Preprints have expanded researchers' freedom in communicating research and enabled new forms of public interaction. Preprint feedback focuses on science rather than journal-specific requirements, allows flexible participation (individual comments or collective reviews), and could enable recognition of reviews as scholarly contributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are based on established knowledge about preprint platforms and their capabilities, representing accurate characterizations of how preprints have changed scholarly communication. Claim C29 is speculative but logically follows from the preceding claims. The result accurately describes the current state and potential of preprint feedback systems.

results.result: While journal peer review is valued but rarely conversational, scientists actively seek feedback through various informal channels. The FAST principles aim to create a new avenue for scientific communication through preprint feedback that would be accessible to both the scientific community and general public.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 accurately describe current peer review practices and scientific communication patterns based on established knowledge. Claims C33-C34 state the intended purpose and anticipated benefits of the FAST principles. While C34 is speculative about future participation, the overall result coherently articulates the motivation and goals for the FAST principles.

results.result: The community is envisioned as an important stakeholder in preprint review with the ability to engage with comments from authors and reviewers, while bearing responsibility to ensure exchanges remain constructive, inclusive, and positive.
results.evaluation: These claims clearly articulate the authors' vision for community involvement in preprint review and the associated responsibilities. While speculative about future practice, they represent a coherent normative framework that is internally consistent with the FAST principles. The claims are appropriately presented as aspirational rather than empirical.

results.result: New platforms and communities for preprint review are emerging, likely enabling novel approaches to commenting on preprints. As preprint feedback activities expand, the authors expect standards and the FAST principles themselves to evolve to meet changing community needs.
results.evaluation: Claim C19 is based on observable trends in scholarly publishing. Claims C20 and C24 are speculative but represent reasonable expectations about technological development and standard evolution. The result appropriately acknowledges both current developments and anticipated future changes, demonstrating appropriate epistemic humility about the evolving nature of preprint review.
